items.title: Blush Clouded Summit
items.description:
Caspar David Friedrich never showed his wanderer's face — just a back, a cliff, and more mountain than one glance could hold.

In Wanderer above the Sea of Fog (c. 1818), Caspar David Friedrich painted a solitary figure from behind, cloak and cliff edge, looking out over a sea of mist that swallows the whole valley below — the single image that came to define the German Romantic idea of the sublime, that particular mix of awe and smallness nature hands you for free if you stand in the right spot. Painters working a very different tradition on the other side of the world reached for the same trick with a single branch: Hiroshige's 1856 print of the pine at Ueno let one looped branch do the work an entire moon would otherwise need.

Blush Clouded Summit keeps Friedrich's arrangement — a peak too large for the frame, a valley reduced to cloud — but swaps his grey northern fog for something closer to dawn: the mountain lit the colour of the inside of a shell, cloud banked around its base like a tide that never finished arriving, dark forested foothills holding the bottom of the frame, a still lake catching the same pink light below. One flowering branch leans in from the top corner, the way Hiroshige once let a single branch stand in for an entire sky.

Where it lives: a bedroom, a stairwell landing, any wall that benefits from a long look rather than a quick one.

items.title: Digital Stillness
items.description:
In his final years Henri Matisse traded the brush for scissors — he called it carving into color.

Long before his eyesight failed him, pattern was already Matisse's obsession. He grew up in a French silk town, and the fabrics and tabletops in his paintings carried an "alphabet of arabesque" of motifs for decades before he ever cut a single shape from paper.

This piece borrows that same instinct — flowers reduced to flat, confident shapes instead of petals and veins, set against a single field of scarlet, with a hand-decorated blue-and-white vase doing the patterned, structural work his textiles always did. Two tulips, one coral and one blush pink, lean into each other at the crown, and a single cobalt-blue rosebud sits low — the one cool note in a warm arrangement.

Where it lives: a kitchen wall, a breakfast nook, anywhere that wants one confident shot of colour over the quiet stuff.

items.title: Apple Room Surreal
items.description:
In 1952 Magritte filled a bedroom with a comb and a shaving brush the size of furniture.

Personal Values, now at SFMOMA, scales up a comb, a bar of soap, a wine glass and a shaving brush until they stop being useful and start being monuments. Magritte’s own explanation: blown up like that, an object “has specifically lost its social character, it has become an object of useless luxury.” Unlike the Surrealists he’s usually grouped with, his disorientation comes from calm, matter-of-fact scale rather than dream logic.

This print takes the same idea and gives it one object instead of four — a single green apple, rim-lit in red, filling nearly the full height of the room, with a small dark chair at its base as the only scale reference. Nothing else in the space is doing anything strange. The apple is the whole event.

An office or a reading room suits it best — anywhere that could use one good, quiet joke on the wall.

items.title: Ultraviolet Dreamscape
items.description:
An infinity pool's edge isn't an illusion — the water really spills over, into a trough you never see.

The vanishing edge that makes a pool look like it pours straight into the sky is a plumbing trick, not an optical one: the water genuinely overflows a lowered lip into a hidden catchment the width of the pool, then gets pumped straight back in. The horizon disappearing is real engineering doing its job quietly.

This print pushes that trick as far as colour will take it — a black-edged pool cropped at a steep angle, a stone pine and red-flowering shrubs crowding one side, a single cumulus bank filling the rest of the frame in high-key cobalt and white. The most saturated, most joyful read in the series.

Where it lives: a bright room that wants one loud, happy wall, or anywhere the rest of the palette is neutral enough to let this one sing.

items.title: Azure Cliff Horizon
items.description:
Caspar David Friedrich believed the divine lived in every blade of grass fringing a cliff edge.

In 1818, on his honeymoon, he painted the chalk cliffs of Rügen — jagged white rock dropping to a calm sea, figures standing right at the precipice, absorbed in a view too large to take in at once. He wasn't alone in that obsession: J.M.W. Turner filled sketchbook after sketchbook with loose, gestural studies of cliffs and sea, chasing the exact way light breaks across rock rather than the rock itself.

This print stands at that same edge. A single vast cloud bank fills half the sky; a streak of rust-orange mineral staining runs down the cliff face where the rock has weathered; a shelf of turquoise-green clifftop catches the light to one side.

Where it lives: a living room, a home office, any wall that could use a deep breath of scale.

items.title: Celestial Mountain Vista
items.description:
Hokusai painted Mount Fuji with only three colours and left every person out of the frame — the mountain alone was enough.

In 1831 Hokusai began the Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, and one print in the set — Red Fuji — stands apart: no village, no traveller, nothing but the mountain the Japanese have called sacred since long before Shinto had a name for the feeling, home to the kami Konohanasakuya-hime. His contemporary Hiroshige found his own version of reverence in a single pine at Ueno, whose one looped branch stood in for an entire moon.

Celestial Mountain Vista gives the peak nearly the whole frame — the largest, closest mountain in this set — with one broad tree standing where Hiroshige’s pine once stood and a blush meadow replacing the shrine steps. Where Hiroshige’s pine looped a branch into a stand-in moon, this tree keeps the sky honest: a plain, burning red sun sits close beside the summit, exactly what it looks like. Still just the two of them: the tree, and the thing it’s been planted to watch.

It calms best in a bedroom before sleep, or any wall that could use less noise.

items.title: Emerald Tree Horizon
items.description:
One tree, one valley, more sky than either needs — the scale Frederic Edwin Church built a career out of painting.

Frederic Edwin Church returned from Ecuador in 1857 with nine weeks of sketches and turned them into The Heart of the Andes — a canvas so overwhelming he had it lit by gas jets behind silver reflectors in a darkened room, and New York queued for it anyway. Real rainforest giants earn that same commanding read without a single human figure: kapok and ceiba trees brace themselves with buttress roots fanning twenty metres from the trunk, built to hold up a canopy taller than most city buildings in soil too thin to trust.

Emerald Tree Horizon keeps the valley, drops the human scale entirely — one dark canopy braced on a cliff's edge, a crimson dusk burning down into indigo rock, a river just visible as a pale thread far below. No painter, no gas jets, no queue — just the view Church spent a career chasing, held in one quiet frame.

Where it lives: a reading nook, a home office that wants one ambitious wall, anywhere that could use a little more scale than it currently has.

items.title: Balcony Echoes
items.description:
Same street, same two men, a few hours later — the quiet now dusk-red instead of violet.

This is the companion to our Silent Balcony Parade print: the identical architecture, the identical pair of anonymous men on their stacked balconies, caught at a different hour. Magritte used that same doubling trick elsewhere — in The Mysteries of the Horizon (1955), three identical men stand at dusk, each facing a different way, each under his own separate moon. Our pair borrows the device at a smaller scale: two men, one shared sky between them instead of one each.

Where that print holds a cool indigo dusk, this one turns the sky scarlet — the same clothesline below as the only sign anyone else lives on this street, the same quiet distance between two men who could almost hear each other if either spoke.

Hang them separately for a single still moment, or hang them together as two hours of the same evening, left to right.

A reading corner, a hallway that could use one good pause — alone, or beside its cooler twin, for the full hour.

items.title: Vase of Wild Grace
items.description:
Janet Fish spent decades proving a glass jar was never really about the jar.

She painted glass vessels from direct observation over days or weeks, deliberately letting daylight change and complicate what was in front of her — "a jar of jelly was never just a jar of jelly," she said. "It was reflection, refraction, and distortion." Her true subject, by her own account, was light and colour, not the object holding them.

This piece catches exactly that moment: late light raking low across an indigo wall, catching the glass low in its belly and turning it the same cobalt as dusk, while loose orange blooms and bare branches rise above the glass line, almost secondary to what the light is doing beneath them.

Where it lives: a hallway that catches late sun, a reading nook, a wall that earns a second look at different hours.

items.title: Valley of Green Giants
items.description:
A valley wide enough that even the clouds needed their own weather — the same trick of scale Frederic Edwin Church built a reputation on.

When Frederic Edwin Church exhibited The Heart of the Andes in 1859, he staged the canvas like a show in its own right — gas-lit, curtained, built to make Manhattan believe it had travelled to Ecuador without leaving 10th Street. The trees that anchor a real jungle valley like that one work the same trick without an audience: kapok and ceiba fan their roots fifty metres from the trunk altogether, wide enough to carry a canopy that never once thinks about falling.

Valley of Green Giants takes the warmer hour — a coral-rose cloud bank fills the sky, the tree's trunk bends in one soft curve rather than standing straight, and a river you can actually trace in bright blue-green winds through grass-green cliffs instead of staying hidden in shadow. Less indigo, more breath.

Where it lives: a living room that wants one confident focal wall, a stairwell, anywhere a little vertigo would be welcome.

items.title: Floral Light Passage
items.description:
A canyon that photographs itself needs two and a half hours of exact sun. This one keeps the trick and plants flowers in it.

Antelope Canyon, on Navajo land near Page, Arizona, is the most photographed slot canyon on Earth, almost entirely because of what happens inside it for roughly two and a half hours a day — a narrow shaft of direct sun falls between the walls from late March to early October, lighting the dust in the air until the whole passage glows. One image of it sold for $6.5 million; another became a default desktop wallpaper seen by millions who never knew its name.

This passage borrows that same architecture — walls closing in toward a bright, inevitable opening — and plants it with colour the real canyon has never had: a path crowded in pink and coral wildflowers instead of bare sandstone. The small figure walking toward the light, seen only from behind, is an older device than the canyon itself — painters have used exactly that view, a traveller’s back to us, since the early 1800s, to put the viewer inside the walk instead of outside it.

An entry hall gets a destination at the end of it; a reading corner gets somewhere worth walking toward.

items.title: Snowy Sunrise Landscape

Climbers on Fuji don't climb for the summit alone — they climb for the hour the mountain gives them just before it, the one Japanese has its own word for.

Where it lives: an east-facing bedroom, a reading chair that catches the morning, anywhere first light is the best part of the day.

items.title: Cloudborne Staircase Portal
items.description:
The most famous staircase in film history was two staircases wearing a trick of scale. This one keeps the trick, loses the explanation.

It rises dead straight out of dense cloud, the lower steps swallowed in mist before you ever see where they start, and arrives at a single lit doorway with nothing beside it to explain how it got there or what’s through it.

A hallway or landing suits the unresolved, quietly dramatic version of it; a reading nook suits the one that likes a question left open — either way, no explanation included.

items.title: Floating Stone Forest
items.description:
The mountains in Avatar aren't fictional — they're erosion, fog, and a very real forest park in Hunan, China.

Zhangjiajie National Forest Park holds more than three thousand quartz-sandstone pillars, carved over millions of years by erosion alone — they don't float, but the dense fog that regularly fills the canyon makes them read that way for a few minutes at a time. James Cameron's production team has said the Hallelujah Mountains of Pandora drew on exactly this kind of karst formation, Zhangjiajie among them; one real pillar was renamed Avatar Hallelujah Mountain after the film's release. Centuries earlier, Chinese shan shui ink painters had already been drawing peaks that gave up solid ground on purpose — not because mountains floated, but because the genre held that a landscape should show what the painter felt, with fog standing in for everything words couldn't.

Floating Stone Forest keeps that same sleight of hand — stone made weightless by cloud, pillars receding into blue haze at every depth, a single pine holding its ground on the nearest ledge the way sacred mountains have always been painted holding court above everything beneath them. An unseen sun lights the clouds gold from somewhere just out of frame; small waterfalls mark the cliff face below, in case anyone needed proof the rock is still solid underneath all that drifting white.

Where it lives: an entryway, a home office, anywhere that could use a little more sky.

Japan has a word for a tree like this one: sonarematsu, the windswept pine, bent by wind it has survived longer than anyone's been counting.

The tree stands entirely alone here, its bent trunk the only vertical line in an open field of white and lavender wildflowers, the peak rendered so soft and pale it nearly dissolves into its own cloud.

It began as a farmer's read on the season, the first blossoms a signal that planting time had come, long before it became a day for good company outdoors. This hill keeps the idea but drops the crowd. One tree, alone on the crest, carries the whole blossom season by itself — no orchard, no festival, just the one bloom in front of an enormous, soft-lit cloud that seems to answer its shape back from the sky. The light pools gold across the grass in the hour hanami was always really about: before anyone else arrives.

Where it lives: a bedroom that wants one calm, singular thing to look at, or a hallway that could use its own quiet season.

items.title: Negative Space Duo

Two women in backless dresses, heels already pointed at the door — the exit, not the room, is the whole point of this pose.

items.title: Pastel Hills Art Print Set of 2, Countryside Hills Pink Green Duo, Spring Decor
items.description:
Hiroshige mapped Japan’s Tōkaidō road one stop at a time. This duo distills that same restlessness into two — a road still going, a tree that stayed.

The Tōkaidō Road prints (1833–34) turned a simple travel route between Edo and Kyoto into one of the most influential series in Japanese art — fifty-three stations, each print catching the road at a different season, a different hour, a different kind of rain. A single flowering tree earns its own tradition too: the architect Hundertwasser called the trees on his buildings ‘tenants,’ arguing their rent — oxygen, shade, a view worth more than money — entitled each one to room enough to be seen from more than one side.

This duo pairs both instincts in one soft palette of pink and green: a road that keeps moving, caught mid-bend toward a hilltop town, and a blossom tree that has already arrived, holding its ground on a quiet rise. The same gentle spring light settles over each.

Both Pastel Hills prints come as one set, the same size, ready to hang as a pair — 15% less than buying them separately.

A bedroom wall, a dining nook, or any pair of narrow spots wanting a matched, quiet moment — that’s where this duo settles in.

Available in 30×45 cm (12×18 in), 40×60 cm (16×24 in) and 60×90 cm (24×36 in) — both prints in the set come in the size you choose.

items.title: Surreal Night Sky Art Print Set of 3, Bowler Hat Midnight Trio, Vermilion Living Room Decor
items.description:
A Buddha under a red sun, a lone figure keeping watch at dusk, a single tree against a burning sky — one deep navy note, carried three ways.

Carved into every Buddha image is a single raised bump at the crown, a mark the tradition says stands for wisdom itself — the ushnisha, carried through two thousand years of stone and bronze. A few feet along the same wall, a man in a dark suit and bowler hat keeps his own private vigil; surrealist painters used that anonymous, faceless figure again and again as a stand-in for the city and the stranger you pass and never remember, often setting him on a row of twilight balconies each under its own separate sky. And past him, a single tree holds a canyon’s enormity in one frame — the kind of scale nineteenth-century landscape painters like Frederic Edwin Church once lit with gas jets behind silver reflectors because an ordinary room couldn’t do it justice.

One note holds the set together — the same deep midnight blue sits behind the sun, the balcony and the canyon, so the trio reads as a single quiet hour rather than three unrelated scenes.

What’s included: all three Midnight & Vermilion prints, the same size, ready to hang as a trio. This set saves 20% versus buying the three separately.

Hang it somewhere that rewards a second look — a study wall, a stairway landing, anywhere quiet drama beats noise.

items.title: Pool Wall Art Print Set of 3, Above the Clouds Surreal Trio, Dreamlike Living Room
items.description:
Caspar David Friedrich painted a man staring into nothing and called it the sublime. This trio gives you three different edges to stand at.

Friedrich’s Wanderer above the Sea of Fog (c. 1818) set the template for this kind of view: a lone figure looking out over mist that swallows the whole valley below, the single image that came to define the Romantic idea of the sublime. In 1946, Powell and Pressburger built a real staircase connecting Earth and Heaven for the film A Matter of Life and Death — a twenty-foot-wide, 106-step motorised ramp disguised by a mixed-scale trick to look impossibly vast. And the pillars that seem to float through cloud in the third print echo Zhangjiajie National Forest Park in China, home to more than three thousand quartz-sandstone columns that regularly vanish into fog for a few minutes at a time.

The same blush-to-cobalt sky runs over the summit, over the stairway, over the forest of stone, carrying all three into one dreamlike journey left to right rather than three separate scenes.

What’s included: all three Above the Clouds prints, the same size, ready to hang as a trio. This set saves 20% versus buying the three separately.

A living room wall or a bedroom that catches the morning light both suit it — what it wants most is room enough to feel like altitude.
